keyPoints.point: Opens in the present: course, college, and what you build or enjoy
One proof project or internship with an outcome
Two or three specific technologies, named
Closes forward: what you want next
Under two minutes of speech — tight, not a life story
Names the project and what it does
Your specific contribution, not the team's
Concrete numbers or measurable outcome
One difficulty you hit and how you solved it
What you learned or would do differently
Sets up the conflict briefly and neutrally
Your own view stated respectfully
Listened to the other side / data over ego
The resolution and its result
The relationship stayed intact or got stronger
Owns a real failure, specifically
Names the cost honestly
What you changed in your process afterwards
Evidence it worked later
No blame-shifting to teammates
A situation where no one was formally in charge
You stepped up with a concrete action
Others followed or the plan moved
The outcome, ideally measurable
Influence without authority, reflected on
Two or three specific strengths mapped to the role
Proof behind each strength (project, number, time)
Knowledge of what THIS company/role needs
A differentiator, not a generic repeat of the resume
Close: the value you'll add in the first months
Encapsulation — bundling data with methods, hiding internals
Abstraction — exposing behaviour, hiding implementation
Inheritance — reuse through parent-child classes
Polymorphism — one interface, many behaviours, e.g. override
A concrete example that isn't Animal/Something vague
Array: contiguous memory, O(1) index access
Linked list: nodes with pointers, O(1) insert/delete at known node
Array cost: O(n) middle insert/delete, resize cost
List cost: O(n) search, extra memory per node
A concrete choice rule (e.g. frequent index reads → array)
Two pointers moving at different speeds — Floyd's cycle detection
If they meet, a cycle exists
Alternative: a visited set with O(n) memory
Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space for the pointer method
Why the fast pointer must catch up inside a loop (relative speed 1)
Process = own memory space; thread = shares the process memory
Context switch cost: process heavier than thread
Threads communicate via shared state; processes via IPC
A race-condition or deadlock example when sharing state
A real choice: browser tabs vs browser threads, or servers
DNS resolution of the hostname
TCP handshake (and TLS if https)
HTTP request sent; server responds with HTML
Browser renders: parse HTML → DOM, fetch assets, paint
Caching at some layer mentioned
TCP: connection-oriented, ordered, reliable, retransmits
UDP: connectionless, fire-and-forget, no delivery guarantee
UDP real use where speed beats reliability
TCP real use where correctness matters
Trade-off stated plainly (latency/promise)
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
3NF: no transitive dependency of non-key on non-key
Why denormalize: read speed over write consistency
The price of denormalization: update anomalies
Atomicity — all or nothing
Consistency — rules/invariants hold before and after
Isolation — concurrent transactions don't trample
Durability — committed data survives crashes
A concrete example (money transfer) and where you'd relax a rule
Average case O(n log n): partition splits roughly in half, log n levels
Partition works by choosing a pivot and rearranging
Worst case O(n²) when splits are maximally uneven — sorted input with bad pivot
Mitigation: random or median-of-three pivot
In-place (O(log n) stack), unlike merge sort's O(n) buffer
REST = resources addressed by URLs, stateless interactions
Verbs as semantics: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes
Status codes carry outcomes: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
An example endpoint designed properly
Why stateless matters (scaling)
Strength stated with proof, not adjectives
A real weakness, owned — with what you're doing about it
The improvement is visible (practice, system, feedback)
Neither answer sounds scripted or self-flattering
A clear yes/no with honest boundaries
Any constraints stated upfront, not discovered later
Professional and cooperative tone, no over-promising
Reads the bond/shift terms before deciding
Near-term: becoming genuinely good at the craft
Mid-term: ownership, mentoring, or scope
Realistic, connected to THIS role's path
No 'left to start a startup in year one' red flags unless honest and framed
A ready question about the work itself
A question about growth or expectations
No salary/leave questions at this slot unless invited
Shows you researched the company
Anchors on market rate for the role and city, stated calmly
Ranges over exact numbers, with basis
Willingness to discuss after learning the full offer
No apology, no bluffing — informed and flexible
